The kings are defeated at the waters of Merom (verses 1–9)

God's miracles for Israel were intended to encourage the people to act energetically themselves.

In the same way, preaching the gospel against Satan's kingdom was initially accompanied and helped by miracles.

Now that the gospel has been clearly demonstrated to be from God, we depend on his grace in its ordinary operation and use the sword of the Spirit.

God encouraged Joshua.

Fresh dangers and difficulties call for fresh support from the word of God, which is always near us and available in every time of need.

God measures our trials according to our strength and supplies strength according to our trials.

Joshua obeyed God's command to destroy the enemy's horses and chariots. His obedience showed self-denial.

Possessing things on which the worldly heart is tempted to rely can harm faith and fellowship with God.

It is better to lose worldly advantages than endanger our souls through dependence on them.

Hazor is captured and burned (verses 10–14)

The Canaanites had filled the measure of their sins.

As a judgment, God left them to their pride, stubbornness, hostility and Satan's power.

The restraints that might have checked them were removed.

God's providential dealings exposed them to despair.

Through their rebellion, they brought upon themselves the punishment they deserved.

The Israelites carried out the judgment God had commanded through Moses.

The territory is subdued and the Anakim defeated (verses 15–23)

Let God's Israel never fear the descendants of Anak: their fall will come at the appointed time.

The land had rest from war.

That was not a peaceful alliance with the Canaanites, which God had forbidden.

It meant that the Canaanites were no longer at war with Israel.

A better rest remains for God's people. They will enter it after their spiritual warfare is complete.

What happened here fulfilled what God had said to Moses.

When God's word and his works are considered together, each helps explain the other.

If we obey our duty conscientiously, we may trust that God will fulfill his promise.

But believers must never lay aside their armor or expect permanent peace in this life.

As their strength and usefulness grow, they may face more difficult trials.

Yet God will not allow any enemy to attack them before he has prepared them for the struggle.

Jesus Christ lives forever to intercede for his people.

Their faith will not finally fail, however severely Satan may attack.

Even when spiritual conflict is long, sharp and difficult, we can endure patiently through joyful hope.

Before long, the believer will rest from both sin and sorrow in the heavenly Canaan.

Verses 1-9
The wonders God wrought for the Israelites were to encourage them to act vigorously themselves. Thus the war against Satan's kingdom, carried on by preaching the gospel, was at first forwarded by miracles; but being fully proved to be of God, we are now left to the Divine grace in the usual course, in the use of the sword of the Spirit. God encouraged Joshua. Fresh dangers and difficulties make it necessary to seek fresh supports from the word of God, which we have nigh unto us for use in every time of need. God proportions our trials to our strength, and our strength to our trials. Joshua's obedience in destroying the horses and chariots, shows his self-denial in compliance with God's command. The possession of things on which the carnal heart is prone to depend, is hurtful to the life of faith, and the walk with God; therefore it is better to be without worldly advantages, than to have the soul endangered by them. ( [Josh.11.10-Josh.11.14] Jos 11:10-14)
[Josh.11.10-Josh.11.14]
Verses 10-14
The Canaanites filled up the measure of their iniquity, and were, as a judgment, left to the pride, obstinacy, and enmity of their hearts, and to the power of Satan; all restraints being withdrawn, while the dispensations of Providence tended to drive them to despair. They brought on themselves the vengeance they justly merited, of which the Israelites were to be executioners, by the command the Lord gave to Moses.
[Josh.11.15-Josh.11.23]
Verses 15-23
Never let the sons of Anak be a terror to the Israel of God, for their day to fall will come. The land rested from war. It ended not in a peace with the Canaanites, that was forbidden, but in a peace from them. There is a rest, a rest from war, remaining for the people of God, into which they shall enter, when their warfare is accomplished. That which was now done, is compared with what had been said to Moses. God's word and his works, if viewed together, will be found mutually to set each other forth. If we make conscience of our duty, we need not question the performance of the promise. But the believer must never put off his armour, or expect lasting peace, till he closes his eyes in death; nay, as his strength and usefulness increase, he may expect more heavy trials; yet the Lord will not permit any enemies to assault the believer till he has prepared him for the battle. Christ Jesus ever lives to plead for his people, and their faith shall not fail, however Satan may be permitted to assault them. And however tedious, sharp, and difficult the believer's warfare, his patience in tribulation may be encouraged by the joyfulness of hope; for he will, ere long, rest from sin and from sorrow in the Canaan above.

The two kings conquered under Moses (verses 1–6)

New blessings should not make us forget the mercies God gave us earlier.

Nor should the new work he gives us cause us to forget the good work others accomplished before us.

Moses gave part of the land promised to Israel to the two and a half tribes on the east side of the Jordan.

It was rich, fertile land.

But Joshua was to give the rest to Israel's tribes.

In this Henry sees a picture of Christ, the true Joshua, giving the inheritance of heavenly Canaan to all God's spiritual Israel.

The kings conquered under Joshua (verses 7–24)

The record names thirty-one kings defeated by Joshua.

Henry describes Canaan as exceptionally fruitful and pleasant at the time Israel entered it, so that many petty rulers could live there in relative prosperity.

He contrasts that description with the land's condition in his own day.

He interprets its loss of fruitfulness as connected to the Jewish rejection of Christ and appeals to Deuteronomy 29:23.

This is Henry's historical and theological assessment, not an independently verified modern claim about the land or its people.

God's judgments are righteous.

We should also remember that he fulfills his promises.

Let the record of former deliverances teach us gratitude for our own mercies.

Let it also lead us to trust God for the blessings still promised to his church.

So the law has given to some few of God's spiritual Israel worldly blessings, earnests of good things to come; but our Lord Jesus, the true Joshua, provided for all the children of promise spiritual blessings, and the heavenly Canaan.

This shows how fruitful Canaan then was, in which so many chose to throng together. This was the land God appointed for Israel; yet in our day it is one of the most barren and unprofitable countries in the world. Such is the effect of the curse it lies under, since its possessors rejected Christ and his gospel, as was foretold by Moses, [Deut.29.23] De 29:23. The vengeance of a righteous God, inflicted on all these kings and their subjects, for their wickedness, should make us dread and hate sin. The fruitful land bestowed on his chosen people, should fill our hearts with hope and confidence in his mercy, and with humble gratitude.

The territory that remains to be taken (verses 1–6)

Joshua had grown old.

Henry considers him to have been around one hundred years old, but that is an estimate rather than a date stated in this passage.

It is a reminder that even the most useful servants of God must eventually be set aside from active work.

We are all moving toward the end of our earthly lives.

Whatever our hands find to do, we should do it with our strength (Ecclesiastes 9:10).

It is good when people who are advanced in age can look back on fruitful labor and encourage others to continue what remains unfinished.

Joshua still had work to arrange, even though he could not personally conquer all the remaining territory.

God's promises never fail merely because one human worker's strength is ending.

The Lord had promised to drive out the remaining Canaanites and would fulfill that promise at the proper time.

His people nevertheless had to exert themselves and act upon what he promised.

The distribution of land east of the Jordan (verses 7–33)

The territories were assigned to Israel's tribes according to God's direction, not seized merely by whoever was most powerful.

The Lord gives different people their rightful places.

We should accept our own portion with gratitude instead of grasping at what belongs to others.

Under the gospel, Joshua pictures Jesus Christ, who obtains the heavenly inheritance for his people and gives them their share in it.

Moses had already granted Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh land east of the Jordan.

Their possessions were to remain within their appointed boundaries.

They had no right to claim additional land merely because God had shown them favor.

The Levites, unlike the other tribes, did not receive an ordinary territorial inheritance.

The Lord himself was their inheritance (Numbers 18:20).

Those serving in sacred ministry should not be driven by desire for riches or entangled in worldly concerns.

The community ought to provide for their legitimate needs, allowing them to devote themselves to the work entrusted to them.

We should all seek a better inheritance than earthly wealth.

God himself is a more precious portion than all the possessions we could gain.

At this chapter begins the account of the dividing of the land of Canaan among the tribes of Israel by lot; a narrative showing the performance of the promise made to the fathers, that this land should be given to the seed of Jacob. We are not to pass over these chapters of hard names as useless. Where God has a mouth to speak, and a hand to write, we should find an ear to hear, and an eye to read; and may God give us a heart to profit! Joshua is supposed to have been about one hundred years old at this time. It is good for those who are old and stricken in years to be put in remembrance of their being so. God considers the frame of his people, and would not have them burdened with work above their strength. And all people, especially old people, should set to do that quickly which must be done before they die, lest death prevent them, [Eccl.9.10] Ec 9:10. God promise that he would make the Israelites masters of all the countries yet unsubdued, through Joshua was old, and not able to do it; old, and not likely to live to see it done. Whatever becomes of us, and however we may be laid aside as despised, broken vessels, God will do his own work in his own time. We must work out our salvation, then God will work in us, and work with us; we must resist our spiritual enemies, then God will tread them under our feet; we must go forth to our Christian work and warfare, then God will go forth before us.
[Josh.13.7-Josh.13.33]
Verses 7-33
The land must be divided among the tribes. It is the will of God that every man should know his own, and not take that which is another's. The world must be governed, not by force, but right. Wherever our habitation is placed, and in whatever honest way our portion is assigned, we should consider them as allotted of God; we should be thankful for, and use them as such, while every prudent method should be used to prevent disputes about property, both at present and in future. Joshua must be herein a type of Christ, who has not only conquered the gates of hell for us, but has opened to us the gates of heaven, and having purchased the eternal inheritance for all believers, will put them in possession of it. Here is a general description of the country given to the two tribes and a half, by Moses. Israel must know their own, and keep to it; and may not, under pretence of their being God's peculiar people, encroach on their neighbours. Twice in this chapter it is noticed, that to the tribe of Levi Moses gave no inheritance: see [Num.18.20] Nu 18:20. Their maintenance must be brought out of all the tribes. The ministers of the Lord should show themselves indifferent about worldly interests, and the people should take care they want nothing suitable. And happy are those who have the Lord God of Israel for their inheritance, though little of this world falls to their lot. His providences will supply their wants, his consolations will support their souls, till they gain heavenly joy and everlasting pleasures.

The inheritance of the nine and a half tribes (verses 1–5)

The Israelites had to settle the land they had conquered. Conquering Canaan would have served little purpose if they did not go on to live there.

Yet each person was not free to choose any place that appealed to him. God would choose their inheritance.

Let us consider both the mercies God has already given us and the inheritance he has promised us—the eternal home in heaven.

Does God show favoritism? Is it not better to have our earthly happiness and suffering assigned by the infinite wisdom of our heavenly Father than by our own ignorance?

Christ has revealed the great mystery of godliness, and Jesus Christ has purchased our redemption. Those who have received such grace should gladly entrust their earthly affairs to the Father's wise arrangement.

Caleb receives Hebron (verses 6–15)

Caleb asked Joshua, “Give me this mountain”—that is, Hebron. God had promised it to him before, and Caleb wanted Israel to see how highly he valued that promise.

Those who live by faith prize what God has expressly promised more than what they receive merely through his providential care.

The Anakim still possessed Hebron. By asking for it, Caleb showed that he was not afraid of those enemies. He also intended to encourage Israel to continue its conquests.

Caleb lived up to his name, which Henry explains as meaning “all heart.” Hebron was granted to Caleb and his descendants because he had followed the Lord God of Israel wholeheartedly.

Happy are we if we follow the Lord in the same way. Exceptional faithfulness will be crowned with exceptional favor.

God shall choose our inheritance for us. Let us survey our heritage of present mercy, our prospect for the land of promise, eternal in the heavens. Is God any respecter of persons? Is it not better that our place, as to earthly good or sorrow, should be determined by the infinite wisdom of our heavenly Father, than by our own ignorance? Should not those for whom the great mystery of godliness was exhibited, those whose redemption was purchased by Jesus Christ, thankfully refer their earthly concerns to his appointment?

Caleb's request is, "Give me this mountain," or Hebron, because it was formerly in God's promise to him, and he would let Israel knows how much he valued the promise. Those who live by faith value that which is given by God's promise, far above what is given by his providence only. It was now in the Anakims' possession, and Caleb would let Israel know how little he feared the enemy, and that he would encourage them to push on their conquests. Caleb answered to his name, which signifies "all heart." Hebron was settled on Caleb and his heirs, because he wholly followed the Lord God of Israel. Happy are we if we follow him. Singular piety shall be crowned with singular favour.

Judah's boundaries (verses 1–12)

Before Israel left Gilgal, Joshua assigned the inheritances of Judah, Ephraim and the half-tribe of Manasseh.

Later the people moved to Shiloh, where another survey was made and the other tribes received their portions.

In due time, all God's people will be settled in the inheritance prepared for them.

Caleb and his daughter Achsah (verses 13–19)

Achsah received land as a free gift from her father Caleb.

But it was land in the south, dry and easily parched.

She asked for more, and Caleb gave her both the upper and the lower springs.

Some understand the description as referring to a single field watered by rain from heaven and by springs rising from the ground.

This interpretation supports a familiar spiritual application.

When we pray, we may seek blessings for our souls and for heaven—the upper springs—and also blessings for our bodies and present lives—the lower springs.

Both kinds of blessing belong to God's children.

Through their relationship to Christ, they receive them freely from their Father as part of their inheritance.

The cities of Judah (verses 20–63)

This passage lists Judah's cities.

But Bethlehem is not named, though it later became David's city and was honored as the birthplace of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Even at its greatest, Bethlehem was a little place among Judah's towns (Micah 5:2).

At this time it was apparently so small that it was not included among the cities listed.

The sons of Joseph.

Ephraim's inheritance

This chapter and the next should be read together. They describe the inheritances of Ephraim and Manasseh, Joseph's sons.

Next to Judah, these tribes were to receive a place of honor. They therefore received the first and best portions in northern Canaan, just as Judah received its portion in the south.

God's people continue, as in earlier times, to allow his enemies to remain.

Blessed Lord, when will all our enemies finally be subdued? The last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Corinthians 15:26). Drive them all out; you alone can do it.

The boundaries of these inheritances remind us that our circumstances and provision during this life, as well as our inheritance to come, are appointed by the only wise and righteous God.

We should therefore be content with our portion. He knows what is best for us, and everything we have is more than we deserve.

Manasseh's inheritance (verses 1–6)

Manasseh was one of Joseph's two tribes, yet its inheritance was divided into two parts.

Zelophehad's daughters now received the benefit of their godly zeal and prudent foresight.

Those who take care, while traveling through this world's wilderness, to secure a place among the saints in light will enjoy the comfort of that inheritance in the next world.

But those who neglect it now will lose that blessing forever.

Lord, teach us to believe and obey here, and grant us an inheritance among your saints in eternal glory.

Manasseh's boundaries and the remaining Canaanites (verses 7–13)

The lands of Manasseh and Ephraim were closely connected.

Although each tribe had its own inheritance, their people could live among one another and show each other kindness.

They belonged to different tribes but were still one Israel, bound to love one another as brothers.

Yet they allowed the Canaanites to remain among them.

They did this against God's command, because it suited their own interests.

Joseph's descendants request more land (verses 14–18)

Joshua held public office and did not favor his own tribe over any other.

He governed without partiality or favoritism. Everyone entrusted with public responsibilities should follow his example.

Joshua told Joseph's descendants that their allotted land would be sufficient if they were willing to work and fight for it.

People invent many excuses to avoid hard work.

One especially convenient excuse is to rely on influential or wealthy relatives who might provide what we want.

We may then press those relatives to use positions of trust unfairly on our behalf.

But it is far kinder to point out opportunities that are already within someone's reach and encourage that person to use them than to encourage laziness and extravagance.

True religion never excuses such behavior.

The rule remains that those unwilling to work should not eat.

Many of the things we claim we “cannot” do are really things our laziness has made us reluctant to attempt.

This happens particularly in our spiritual work and warfare.

Apart from Christ we can do nothing.

But instead of trusting him and acting, we may simply sit still and attempt nothing.

If we truly belong to Christ, he will stir us to make our best efforts and cry to him for help.

Then our territory will be enlarged (1 Chronicles 4:9–10), and our complaints will cease—or better, become joyful thanksgiving.

The tabernacle is established at Shiloh (verse 1)

Shiloh lay within the territory of Ephraim, Joshua's own tribe. It was fitting for the tabernacle to be near the chief governor's home.

The city's name was the same as the name used in Jacob's prophecy about the Messiah (Genesis 49:10).

Some have suggested that the city received this name when it was chosen as the resting place of the ark. The ark pictured our great Peacemaker and the way he opens for us to approach a God reconciled to us.

The remaining land is surveyed (verses 2–10)

After a year or more, Joshua rebuked the people's delay and told them how to proceed.

Through his grace, God has given us a claim to a good land—the heavenly Canaan. Yet we are often slow to take possession of what he offers.

We fail to enter fully into the rest that we might already enjoy through faith, hope and holy joy.

How long will we continue hindering our own happiness and exchanging God's mercies for empty, deceitful things?

Joshua urged the Israelites to take possession of the lands assigned to them. He was prepared to do his part if they would do theirs.

Benjamin's boundaries (verses 11–28)

Each tribe's portion had its boundaries drawn clearly and its inheritance settled.

God's wise appointment prevented arguments and selfish demands.

He distributed the hills and valleys, fields of grain and pasture, streams and rivers, towns and cities.

If a servant of Christ receives a portion of affliction and sorrow, it comes under the Lord's authority. Let the Lord do what seems good to him.

If we receive prosperity and peace, they also come from above.

We should be humbled when we compare our gifts with how little we deserve them.

Never forget the One who gives good things, and always be willing to surrender them when he commands.

Simeon's inheritance (verses 1–9)

Judah's people did not object when towns within their assigned territory were given to Simeon, once they understood that they had received more than was right.

If a true believer has gained an advantage improperly, even without intending it, that believer will give it up without complaining.

Love does not insist on its own interests or behave shamefully.

Where love dwells richly, it leads us to share what belongs to us with brothers and sisters who lack what they need.

Zebulun's inheritance (verses 10–16)

The division of land among Israel's tribes fulfilled the prophetic blessings spoken by Jacob.

Whether the people chose their portions or received them by lot, their inheritance was assigned in the places Jacob had foreseen.

How trustworthy the prophetic word is! It teaches us what to believe and confirms the truths God has revealed.

The other tribes and Joshua's own inheritance (verses 17–51)

Joshua waited until every other tribe had settled before asking for any land for himself.

He was content to have no settled place until the people were provided for.

This is a model for everyone serving in public office: place the common good before personal advantage.

Those who work hardest to benefit others should seek an inheritance in the heavenly Canaan.

It will be soon enough to enter that inheritance when they have completed all the service they can offer their brothers and sisters.

Nothing gives them greater assurance of their own inheritance than seeking to help others desire, seek and receive it.

Our Lord Jesus came to live on earth in poverty rather than splendor.

He provided rest for humanity while having no place to lay his own head.

Christ did not seek to please himself.

Nor did he enter his own inheritance until, through obedience even to death, he had secured the eternal inheritance for all his people.

He will not count his own glory complete until every person he has redeemed has entered heavenly rest.

Israel appoints the cities of refuge (verses 1–6)

Once the Israelites had settled in the inheritance promised them, God reminded them to set apart cities of refuge.

The purpose and symbolic meaning of those cities had already been explained in Numbers 35 and Deuteronomy 19.

God's spiritual Israel has, and will continue to have, not only rest in Christ and heaven, but also a refuge where people can find safety.

These cities pictured the relief the gospel provides for repentant sinners.

In our Lord Jesus Christ, those who flee to him find protection from the law's curse and God's wrath (Hebrews 6:18).

The six refuge cities (verses 7–9)

The cities on both sides of the Jordan were positioned so that, from any part of the country, a person could reach one within half a day's journey.

God is always a refuge near at hand.

All six were Levite cities.

This arrangement was a kindness to fugitives. Someone who could not go up to the Lord's house would nevertheless have God's servants nearby to teach, pray and help make up for the lack of regular public worship.

Some interpreters also find spiritual meaning in each city's name:

Kedesh means holy: our Refuge is the holy Jesus.

Shechem means shoulder: the government rests on his shoulder.

Hebron means fellowship: believers are brought into fellowship with Jesus Christ our Lord.

Bezer means fortification: he is a stronghold for everyone who trusts in him.

Ramoth means high or exalted: God has exalted Christ at his right hand.

Golan means joy or exultation: in him all the saints are justified and will rejoice in his glory.

Verses 7-9
These cities, as those also on the other side Jordan, stood so that a man might in half a day reach one of them from any part of the country. God is ever a Refuge at hand. They were all Levites' cities. It was kindness to the poor fugitive, that when he might not go up to the house of the Lord, yet he had the servants of God with him, to instruct him, and pray for him, and to help to make up the want of public ordinances. Some observe a significance in the names of these cities with application to Christ our Refuge. Kedesh signifies holy, and our Refuge is the holy Jesus. Shechem, a shoulder, and the government is upon his shoulder. Hebron, fellowship, and believers are called into the fellowship of Christ Jesus our Lord. Bezer, a fortification, for he is a strong hold to all those that trust in him. Ramoth, high or exalted, for Him hath God exalted with his own right hand. Golan, joy or exultation, for in Him all the saints are justified, and shall glory.
